title: A Undertow for the Radiators
premise: Tamsin Dunmore, a translator who has spent thirty years in England quietly losing the Cornish of his childhood, learns that the house in Porthleven where his mother once kept a boarding house is going to auction. Returning to catalogue its contents — and the unsaid words of his estranged brother Merrick — he uncovers letters revealing why his mother sent him away, and that Merrick has been keeping the language alive in his absence. As bidding day approaches, Tamsin must choose between the safe, wordless life he has built and claiming both the house and the tongue that made him. He loses the auction but wins back the language, reading his mother's letters aloud in Cornish on the empty doorstep while Merrick, for the first time, answers.
about_author: Dominic Ashgrove is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who grew up between coastal England and inland Wales, writing quietly about language, loss, and the houses we cannot re-enter. His work has appeared in small literary journals, and this is his second novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Tamsin, translating a dull shipping contract in his London flat, realises he can no longer recall the Cornish word for 'hearth' and begins a notebook of everything slipping away. A solicitor's letter arrives: the Porthleven house is auctioned in three weeks. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as professional detachment.

chapters.title: Salt in the Doorframes
chapters.summary: Tamsin returns to the shuttered house to prepare it for viewing and runs into Merrick, who refuses to help and speaks to him in fluent Cornish — a small cruelty that cuts deep. Among the attic boxes Tamsin finds a bundle of his mother's unposted letters addressed to him. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: resentment curdling into hunger.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Reading the letters by lamplight, Tamsin learns his mother sent him to an English aunt to shield him from his father's debts, and that Merrick stayed and chose her silence as loyalty. At the auction preview, brothers argue publicly; Merrick accuses Tamsin of coming back only to translate the past into something painless. POV: Tamsin, with one letter in Merrick's voice. Emotional beat: the climax — grief spoken aloud at last.

chapters.title: Undertow, Turning
chapters.summary: Tamsin loses the house to a developer but stays for the clearing sale, reading his mother's final letter aloud in Cornish on the doorstep. Merrick, watching, corrects one word of his pronunciation — then another — and stays to help carry out the last boxes. The notebook of lost words gets its final entry: hearth. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: resolution — belonging rebuilt in language, not walls.
